projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Lawrence Verga was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: In 1941 I was living in Beaver Falls, Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: Seventeen, I had just graduated from high school. And I was going to college. I worked 4:00 to 12:00 and went to college in the mornings. I lived about three blocks away from the college and right across the street from the factory, so it made it kind of handy. And they were desperate for people to work anyway because everybody was leaving in the service. So I did that for a year and a summer. And then I decided to volunteer for the service then. And one of the reasons that I did was -- actually, there was about three of us. They were taking everybody -- you could volunteer to be drafted. So they were taking everybody, and everybody was going into the Navy whether they wanted to or not. And I thought, with my eyesight not being too good, that I could -- they would still put me in the Navy. So I went to the draft board and said, "Take me in the next batch," and that was in July of '43.

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: Yeah. Okay. And then so since there was just one other son that was -- my brother was already in the Navy. My father had passed away, oh, about a week before Pearl Harbor. And so I was sort of responsible for my mother. And so they wouldn't take me until I went home and -- said I had to sign an affidavit that she could get along on thirty bucks a month. So I did that. And the irony of the thing was, it wasn't too long after I was in the service that they raised the dependency allotment to fifty bucks, but they never gave it to my mother. They never gave me the fifty dollars. But I was -- but anyway, I go to the recruitment center, the induction center, rather. And what happened was, there were four of us; two wanted the Marines and two wanted the Navy. So I wound up, I had the Army. And the reason was, my eyesight. So they said limited service. If you are limited service and you are a big husky guy, they make an MP out of you; otherwise, they make a medic out of you. So then I wound up in the medics. The other friend -- I had two friends. The one wanted the Marines and the one wanted the Navy with me. Both wound up in the Army. And the other one, he got what he wanted, he went into the Marines. And unfortunately, poor old Joe, he got -- he wound up getting his elbow shot away on Iwo Jima. And the other two, I ran into -- so we went to -- god, I can't -- the induction center in Maryland, I can't think of the name of it right now. But anyway, we wound up in the same camp, not knowing that, and that was Camp Edwards in Massachusetts. They were in an antiaircraft outfit, and I wound up in an ambulance company. So I had to learn to drive ambulances. And I ran into them. And one weekend that we got off, we went to New York City for the weekend. But, anyway, I thought that was odd that we would wind up there. I stayed there. I had a medical basic in that ambulance company. And then I asked the guy -- I heard about ASTP. And he said, well, yeah, you have to finish basic and then we will see what happens. So they sent me to a -- what they call a star unit, and that was at City College in New York City. And so I went down there, and I took my tests and everything and passed and all of this and just waited for an assignment. So they usually -- they usually tried to send you to a college or university near your home. So I figured maybe I'd go to Carnegie Tech in Pittsburgh, you know. But on that day when I saw my name on the bulletin board and said I was leaving, you know, I got myself some candy and a paperback book to read. And the next thing you know, I am on the back of a two-and-a-half-ton truck going right across the Manhattan Bridge. He says, "You are here, Pratt Institute in Brooklyn, New York." So I was going into basic engineering. And I was there for a semester. And I think the alphabet from T to Z, I was the only one that passed. Unfortunately, they closed up that program and slapped us all in the infantry. So I am walking the streets of New York one day, and three days later, I got a full-filled pack in a down-pouring rain in Camp Hope, Louisiana, walking across the Sabine River. But when I get down there, in the infantry, you know, I didn't go from a bale of hay. So he said, "What do you want?" And I said, "Well, somebody told me if you are in the antitank you ride instead of walk." He says, "Okay. Give him the antitank." So that is how I wound up as an antitanker. But anyway, after basic, after maneuvers with the 75th Division, they decided to take all us replacements from the colleges, and they took the other people that were in there, and they kept a cadre and they sent the other ones to -- what they call that? -- rebel depots. And the -- we went -- no, no, we were sweating it out. I felt we were going to go to Camp Shelby in Mississippi, but I really didn't want to -- I didn't like the South. So, fortunately, we wind up at Camp Breckenridge in Kentucky. And, of course, that was right across the Ohio River from Evansville, that was more you were still more or less up in the North. So I stayed there for an infantry basic. So I was there and went through an infantry basic. And that was that summer. And then around October, we prepared to ship overseas. Oh, incidentally, we filled up the division with these guys from the Air Corps. And they were all going to colleges too and everything, and they cut out that program. And we all wound up in the infantry. So we filled out the division that way. And then we prepared, I think in the end of October, we went to Camp Shanks in New York and from there over to Europe. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In October of '44 or '43?

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: That would be' 44, October of '44. And what was unusual, I went on the Edmund B. Alexander; that was a German ship captured in World War I, see. So somewhere in their minds, they -- I had gotten -- written something or anyway -- but they thought I was a painter. So I get on the ship, and I get a call one day and the guy says -- said I could go down there. I said, "What, are we going to paint signs or something?" He says, "No, we are going to paint the ship." So every day, there I was by the bucket of paint, painting this ship. And I'm talking about we painted everything. And they would have -- they would have boxing matches on the hatch covers. And these guys would be standing and staring, and they would be standing right on things we had just painted. So we would go along and, while they were looking up, we would paint their shoes. Anyway, we were in a big convoy when we went over there at that time. But I worked the same hours as -- it was a -- it was operated by the British, guarded by the U.S. Marines, and run by U.S. Seamen, Merchant Marine. And so I talked the guy into working exactly the same hours as the merchant seamen, see. And, hey, those guys had a coffee break at 10:00. So we had a coffee break and knocked off at 3:00. Then I got one better. I told the guys, I says, "Hey, since I am doing this work, I am coming to your quarters for a shower instead of taking a saltwater shower." Okay. I remember the first time I went down there. Every time you opened the door, the lights would go out, you know, from blackout regulations. So it took me a while before I figured that out. I went inside and the light came back on again, so I was okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In the meantime, you wouldn't go in because the lights were out?

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: Right. But it was -- that painting was good duty because, if you didn't have that, you would be on KP, and working in the mess hall was terrible because -- especially when you were still under blackout conditions and they didn't have portals open and stuff like that. Man, a little air and you had to boil in the seawater because you ate with the mess kits. And, of course, your quarters, you were all stacked up about fifteen high on cots. But, anyway, like I said, that was a good duty. But my fatigues, by the time I got over there, were so full of paint and everything that they could stand up by themselves. And we landed in the Swansea in Wales. I went through this little town of Narberth. And it was kind of a shock to me; you see lots of houses with thatched roofs. I thought I was back in the Middle Ages somewhere. So we stayed there and got our equipment ready, taking stuff out of Cosmoline and things of that nature. We test-fired our weapons, and then we went over across the Channel and almost coincidentally with the Bulge starting when the Germans attacked. And I went across the channel on an old excursion, cross-channel excursion boat, the Ben-My-Chree. And they stacked us on there where you sat, and you sat with all your gear, your pack and everything. And another guy sat between your legs and another guy between him -- between that, we were just on that deck. I don't know what happened. That is supposed to be about, I don't know, a fifteen-hour trip or something like that. We were on it for three days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get lost?

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: I don't know what happened. But anyway, then we get to Le Havre. And at Le Havre, the Americans had blown the whole port apart, you know, and I don't think the French were very happy about that. But we had to transfer to infantry landing craft that took us up on the beach and dropped you in the water, you know, so that is how we got there. Then we went to a camp in a place called Yvetot and stayed there about a day or two. And then they put us on the Fabulous Forty and Eight, you know, quarante. What is that? You have forty men -- quarante huit chevaux. There we go. And that --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Forces --

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: Yeah, right. And that was a real trip. I want to tell you. And there you were packed in like sardines the same way, with a guy sitting there right next to you with all your -- now we had our gear, too, because then we had our -- all our gear. What do you call it? The AMB bag. And to go to the bathroom was something else when I got there. And I remember I had -- I had to go in the town of Valenciennes right in the middle of the station, so I crawled out, managed to crawl out and I crawled up on a freight train. And I don't know which way it was going, but it was stopped. So I did my business, and I was sitting there wondering which train was going to leave first. And another thing that happened while we were going there, the train would stop and you would hear this noise. It was a buzz bomb, and sometimes you would hear a big thud in the distance. But that was my first experience -- well, it really wasn't because I went -- I went to -- while we were in Wales, one weekend I got a pass and went to London. And I must be a sound sleeper, because the next day, my buddy and I woke up and there was a hole in the ground next door. I don't know whether it was planes or whatever bombed it, but it was gone.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Slept right through it?

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: Yeah, I slept right through it -- slept right through it. Slept right through it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. So how long were you in England before you went over the Channel, crossed the Channel?

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: Just about a month. Yeah. And, incidentally, probably we left there, oh, probably like the first week of December and the Bulge started about the 15th of December. And I think it was -- that is the last time I had a bath until the following March or February, it was. But anyway, we get up to -- we were going to join Simpson and the 9th Army, which would be the northernmost Americans next to the British in the northernmost American sector. But they delayed us and -- the Bulge occurred and, of course, that delayed us and we couldn't get up there anyway. So what happened, we just joined -- I forget who it was. I think it was some armored outfit. Our division never fought -- until January the 15th, our division -- the regiments were attached to other outfits, an armored outfit, another infantry division or something like that. Never fought as a division until January of '45 in the Bulge. But prior to that -- anyway, we got our first taste. We moved in a town -- I can't think of the name. Oh, Vielsalm. We moved into this town of Vielsalm, and we take over for -- it had to be an armored outfit because they made so much noise leaving. And the Germans, every time they heard that noise, they would throw shells over. And I don't think we were there ten minutes when our first guy -- we had our first casualty when a guy went diving to the ground and he got hit in the back with a piece of shrapnel. So we stayed there for -- and after we left that, then we moved to the area where Grand-Halleux is. And that is, I told you, the first time we went in as a division. And Grand-Halleux -- that's a small town. It is sort of -- it is sort of on a hill. And there's one road that goes east and one road that goes sort of -- no, west and one road that sort of goes northeast, see. Well, the first battalion, we went up on the northeast, and the second battalion went west. And they went up the hill to the west. And there was a big church at the bottom of the hill, and kind of the road is divided into a Y, and they went up. The way we went, there was a machine gun pinning everybody down and was kind of raking the street, you know. And that's when I ducked into the house. I still have that picture of the house that I ducked into. I didn't know what -- I picked up this card in the house, and then I stuck it in my pocket. And when I got out in the daylight and I looked at it, it was a postcard of the town. And it had the very house that I was in was in the corner of the shot, of the community, you know, a postcard from 1930. But, anyway, my son said it was like having a cameraman with you. But, anyway, I found out later, this machine gun -- I found out later. I was at a reunion in Atlanta with -- well, he went from Captain Bogardus to major to colonel, whatever. At the time he was leading Charlie Company, which was leading the attack. And I got pinned down. He called in coordinates that were so accurate that artillery blew that machine gun out of -- and then we just moved on and there was hardly any casualties, and we had no problem. However, the second battalion that went up that other hill, they endured about a hundred casualties. They had about fifty guys killed and at least that many wounded, going the other way. I had never known those stories. You know, I find out those things afterwards, because when you are there -- when you are actually in battle like that, you don't know anything that is going on outside of your squad. You don't even know what the other squad is doing, in other words. And I found that out too by talking to my friends after the war. And I see them now whenever I go back to reunions of the 75th, you know. And I will say, "Where in the heck were you?" "I didn't go over on that Ben-My-Chree." I said, "Where did you go?" He said, "Oh, I went with the equipment." I says, "I went with our guns and everything on an LST," you know what I mean? I didn't know. That is another one -- and I said, "Where were you?" And the guy says, "I got pneumonia, was in the hospital." He says, "I never came back to the outfit until spring," you know. So you really didn't know what was going on beyond your own little group. I had something happen before we attacked Grand-Halleux. We moved in in the dark and we set up our antitank to cover this main road that went across this bridge into Grand-Halleux. And, I mean, it was below zero and the snow was up to your knees. I mean, it was freezing. And I get up in the morning, and here comes this Jeep down the hill. And who was in the Jeep? The division exec, the general. What the heck was his name? Prickett, Prickett was the commander and this other one was the exec. I forget -- Mickle -- I forget what his name was now. But, anyway, he said, "Where is the road?" And I said -- "Now I am in command." But this I found out later too. I said, "Sergeant Murphy is." "Where in the hell is Sergeant Murphy?" He is the platoon leader or squad leader. He said -- he went on sick call. And he said he saw that Jeep coming down the road and he hid in the bushes, left me there to take the rap. So the general in his Jeep says, "Where is the road?" I said, "I don't know." We come in in the dark. It stops here. You see a fence and everything, see, like it dead-ended. So he said, "There's supposed to be a road here." I said, "Well, if it's marked on the map, might be, but I don't see any road." So he said, well -- he decides he is going to cut right across in front of us, in the snow, leave the tracks. You are not supposed to do things like that. But, anyway, he said, "Move that gun." That was a sixty-four thousand dollar question. We couldn't budge it; it was frozen in place. All of his assistants had to jump out of the Jeep; we couldn't move it. So he just takes his Jeep; he is real mad. Oh, first he chewed me out. I was putting my hands in my pocket. He chewed me out because I lost my gloves, and it was really cold. So, anyways, he says, "Don't put your hands in your pocket when you talk to me." And he says, "What is down there?" And I said, "Well, we -- one of our tanks is on that main road that goes in there and stopped. And the tanker says that the road is mined between there and the bridge." So that is it. He says, "Don't let any tanker tell you; you are an infantryman." Then they get in their Jeep and, zoom, right across and leave all these tracks for the luftwaffe to find. But, anyway, this is about maybe ten minutes later. Here comes General Prickett; he is the commander. Now, he was more like -- he was more like fatherly. He slapped my shoulder, and he says, "Where is your men?" I says, "In the foxholes, sleeping; it is cold." So he says, "Hey, you have got to get your men working," says "they are happier when they are moving and working." Well, that was the end of it. He takes off in the same direction as Mickle -- I can't think of his name; I think it is Mickle. But, anyway, it was twenty minutes later; here he come back again. I can still see the scowl on their faces as they zoom past us and go up the hill. And, of course, they went up to headquarters, chewed everybody out up there. But I had never -- I had never seen a general, and here I had two in a row, chewed out by two. Whether that was a distinction in the U.S. Army -- anyway, I lived through that. Then we took off and attacked the town on across that bridge. And, like I said, then we went up the streets where the machine guns -- from that point, we -- when we left that town, we entered a patch -- a force. You know, it's the Ardennes woods. And those are tall pine trees. And, of course, everything was snow laden and everything else and then digging foxholes and snow falling off the trees; you are wet, you are -- it is cold and everything else. But we managed -- we went through the woods and finally we kept going east. And my last recollection was standing on the edge of the woods and looking down into the town of Commanster and seeing in a shadow a building that was -- on a German tank, so I just assumed that there would be a tiger tank all painted white sitting down there. And that was my last recollection of the Battle of the Bulge there. But, prior to that, one morning -- oh, before that too, even in Vielsalm, he appointed me as a runner. So I go from my squad back to headquarters and find out any messages and then come back. And they had this -- they had this -- this street went up and sort of dead-ended into a field. And then you had this other road that went off to the east. And that was it, that little corner. But the Germans were across the field. And every time they saw a motion over there, they would throw shells. And what brought that on, when we -- when we moved in was all that -- excuse me -- all that noise of that armored -- you know, because it was an armored outfit and they were moving their tanks out and all this stuff. Anyway, the first house we went in there got hit with a shell and started burning, so we just moved to the next one. But a sad thing happened was, there was an old couple in the house, probably in their seventies or eighties, and the man was scared. And he broke away from us while no one was watching him, and he got out of the house and ran down the street to that corner. And sure enough, as soon as that motion -- he got killed there. The Germans threw in shells, and he got killed. There were dead cows and everything else laying there, you know, from -- like I said, anytime they come -- anyway, I was a runner and I would stay away from that street. So I go down parallel to the street, but I go through the fields, through a cemetery and down to headquarters, and then I would run back the other way. So when I was coming back, we had a hell of a barrage that came in. So I am laying there, hugging these tombstones and worrying about -- I knew fellow GIs were in those houses and everything. So you are taking a chance that somebody doesn't take a buckshot at you on the way. But after I got back, the sergeant says, "Hey, you are not supposed to be doing that," he says, "because you are the gunner." So he said, "Give that job to Rennie." Okay. So Rennie does the same thing I did. He comes back and in one of those barrages -- and a piece of shrapnel hits him in the toe. All it did was tear his boots and made his big toe black and blue, see. And we always talk about that because I still talk to him; he lives in Boston. I said, "Don't you remember, and you didn't go get a Purple Heart, see, and you sacrificed five points," but nobody knew you were going to get five points at the time. Another interesting development with Rennie and I, it was a blizzard and it was -- snow was coming down like crazy and it was dark, and it must have been 4:00 or 5:00 in the morning. So we duck in this house to get out of the snow for a while. And we duck in this house and, lo and behold, what is in it? There is a medic taking care of two German PWs that had been wounded, you know. And, of course, he is screaming, and I just assume it was Yiddish, but he is screaming, you know, "Master race" and all this, and "I am a Jew, and I am fixing you up" and all of this kind of stuff, see. So then Rennie sees this one guy, and he apparently wasn't wounded too badly, this one. And he sees he is wearing a rabbit fur vest. So he says -- he decides to appropriate it for himself. That was bad news. So he put it on. You know, it is full of lice. So he is sitting there, and the German is catching it -- is smashing -- smashing the lice on a C ration can. See, he had to take that stupid -- then the guy said, he says, "Well, we haven't had a change of underwear since September." That was the German. Well, we are sitting there and not very long and the other guy just falls over dead. So he must have been wounded somewhere that he didn't let on, you know. Anyway, he just toppled over, so we hauled him out and threw him in the snow, and that was it. But, anyway, then we moved on and then after -- after that, we wondered what was going to happen. And they sent us down to near Colmar, France because there was a pocket of Germans still in Colmar. So they sent us down there, and we joined the French First Army. And they had the, I think, the 28th Division and our division and some armored outfits, whatever. And it was -- I think it was the 24th Army Corps, but anyway, we were attached to the French First Army down there. Oh, let me -- just as a sidebar on that, we went in -- we went into -- we went into battle with the regular garrison equipment that you wear here in the States, you know. All we had was these boots, galoshes-like, and our regular garrison shoe, no winter equipment whatsoever. What I used to do was, when I would get issued a pair of long johns, I would put the clean pair next to my skin and pull all the rest of them up on top. Another thing I tried to do was make sure that I took my shoes off at least once a day because your feet sweat and you wind up getting trench foot and everything else. So I never had any problems in that direction. However, it was June before I could take a shower without my feet stinging from the cold because when we got -- after Colmar, they issued us combat boots -- no, prior to that, they issued us snow packs. But, hey, you know, in France, it was spring already and it was warm. And so now they come with the snow shoes. And those were even worse because they had rubber bottoms and leather tops. And if you put -- and your feet really sweat and perspired in those. So on those things I used to throw straw, paper, anything that I could in there because they also didn't give us -- they would give us the felt pads that went in the bottom, so there we are without the felt pad. So every day I would throw out that lump of wet stuff and put dry stuff in again. So I managed to keep any feet in shape for the whole war. I didn't have any problems. Some of the other guys had frozen feet and stuff like that. But anyway, we were in Wolfgantzen and we attacked the town of Wolfgantzen. And we went in this little -- well, Fortschwihr before that, Fortschwihr, and then we go to Wolfgantzen. We are going down the road and we enter this patch of woods and all hell breaks loose. That is when you are laying on the ground with the tree bursts and motor shells just cutting all the branches. And my buddy jumped off and he went to take off the cover on the muzzle of our antitank gun and he got a piece of shrapnel right through his arm and that was the last I saw of Mike until after the war. So you can get a thousand dollar wound or whatever you want to.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's a million dollar --

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: A million dollar wound, yeah right. And I saw him after he came back to the outfit after the war. I still talk to him. He lives in New York, and he spent all this time in a hospital in Paris and then came back when it was over, see, which is a difference. I was there. I never had a scratch and I was there -- I think our division was in combat a hundred and twenty days. So I didn't miss a day of it. My sergeant, he spent time with pneumonia, so he was gone. And some of the guys had those wounds -- even the fellow, that first guy that got wounded came back to the outfit. But anyway, fighting in Colmar was -- start out at 6:00 in the morning and we repulsed and finally, finally take the town at 6:00 in the evening, see. And, you know, all this fighting is going on. And this was the amazing thing: The day after that, nothing. The Germans had taken off. They retreated across the Rhine River. They wanted to get across the Rhine River, see. So they are fighting 1ike mad one day and the next day wasn't. As a matter of fact, I saw two pieces. I saw that artillery -- I forget what the -- the largest one we had, it came in two pieces, big tractors. And it come rumbling down the road. I had never seen the pieces of our artillery, you know, but that is how quickly the front lines changed there. And there was -- oh, we had Sergeant Bonde. Sergeant Bonde was the platoon leader of the AMP platoon. That is the ammunition and pioneer that gets the ammunition for everybody. He used to wander all over the place. We would see him all the time, you know. He'd come by. I saw him that morning. Then later on I would find out -- then I got this story from that Captain Bogardus when we were talking in Atlanta, and he was saying his platoon leader got killed. And there was Bonde. He climbed up on a tank firing a machine gun and was leading these guys. So Bogardus says, "Hey, would you like to come -- would you like to lead this platoon?" And he said "yes." So immediately he was transferred and got a battlefield commission. But Bonde, Bonde was from Minnesota and he spoke German like a native. He also got the Silver Star and some other things from -- I think he talked in about twenty prisoners into surrendering when we were in the Bulge. Anyway, so we leave -- everything falls apart. Everything is okay. So then we decide to -- -- they were going to ship us north and we don't know where we are going now, so they are shipping us north. And we get to go to a town called Luneville, and that is where they had these quartermaster showers, you know, a minute to get up, a minute to get soaped up and a minute to get out. So Rennie and I were walking down the street and here's a brand new pair of combat boots hanging on a truck that we appropriated. That was about a size twelve, but then we took turns wearing them so we could get rid of those snow packs. Then from there we went to Holland and we joined the British Second Army now and in Holland and the Maas River. But everything was flooded up there, so not too much was going on. But when we took over, the British, they were playing soccer in the streets. Of course, we didn't mess around. And our colonel got killed there and some other guys. They went on patrol. It was like a little island out there on the Maas River and they went out to that island. And he tripped a land mine and it killed a couple of guys besides himself. And Captain Bogardus was with him, and that is another story he told me when he was there that day. He said, "Yes," he says, "I got a little piece of shrapnel in my butt that didn't amount to much," but he told us what happened. So I got that story from him. Of course, we are talking thirty years later, you know what I mean? I didn't know those stories. I just happened to have a conversation with him one day. He was a hell of a guy. He was head of C Company. But after that, we moved to the Rhine River. And what happened was, with the bridge head at Remagen, that kind of loosened everything up after that. And they expected terrific battles and everything to cross the Rhine. But once they had reached the Rhine at Remagen and everything, I think that kind of loosened things up all the way along. So we were to make the northernmost American crossing, even though we were with the British Second Army. So we spent the time in a town on the Rhine River called Buckeburg and did nothing. That was -- for about a week, we did nothing there except -- actually, we did nothing. Oh, we had a couple of things happen while we were there. They decided to come out with a new hand grenade shaped like an apple. And it was a fragmentation grenade and it would explode on contact. And so I don't know why I wasn't there. I wonder why I missed it. So they had everybody come down there and they were demonstrating it. While they were demonstrating, the guy brought the thing back, hit his helmet and it went off. And I remember this sergeant, Sergeant Hooker, who was in another platoon, they tell me he lost his nose, and a couple of guys must have been gotten killed too. But they never issued that hand grenade after that, but that is what happened. In the meantime, all we were doing was we had appropriated a side of beef from the Germans. And, of course, the houses were full of potatoes, so we would just have steak and potatoes. We only went to the mess hall to get coffee and bread. And we happened to be -- oh, we had -- the Navy came in. They came in with these big tractors with these LCIs loaded on them, kind of like bulldozers, bulldozed the road right straight down to the river, you know. In the meantime, whatever was left of the Luftwaffe, the guy comes over, just nuisance value, starts strafing, you know, in the afternoon. So my buddy, he runs out of the house and he gets out in the hallway and don't you know, a bullet ricocheted off. This guy was lucky. Went down through his breast pocket and come out his pant leg and just a scratch on his leg. I told him, I said, "What the hell did you go out there for? Forget about them." Okay. So we -- so then we were preparing to make the crossing. Oh, another thing that happened, we had -- Sergeant Murphy was in his glory because he was a cowboy from Nevada. He had an old nag out there and we had to go around to all of these houses in preparation of all this bombardment and everything that was going to go on and so forth, get the cows and everything out of the barns and all of that. And he was rounding them up out there with his old horse. I say he was in his glory. He was trail boss. But anyway, they decide -- we were going to make the initial crossing and then they decide to put another division, I think the 83rd or another one went through instead of us. There was no resistance there anyway, and the engineers had a pontoon bridge up. By 10:00 in the morning, we were across on the pontoon bridge. So we are still messing around because there is nothing going on. So Sergeant Creech and I, we go along the riverbank and I am walking. And I said, "Wait a minute, stop." Sure enough, he had fortunately stepped over a wire. And that was -- and we -- then we had these guys come and they discovered a whole field of these personnel mines that fly up in the air. And he -- well, like I said, I don't know how he missed it, but he didn't trip it. And I don't know how I saw it. I happened to be looking down and I say, "Hey." But anyway, we go further up that bank. Someone came and marked this whole field with little strips of white cloth, you know, so people would know where not to go. And we were going along the bank and, sure enough, there's a dugout into the bank and there's two dead Germans laying there. Of course, they had all the paraphernalia was laying there, you know, the wires and everything was laying there. So somebody nailed them. I don't know who did. But anyway, there was a houseboat there. So I went on that houseboat and I still have -- I got the company flag off of one end and the Nazi flag off of the other end. And I still have those. Actually, a couple of years ago I decided to find -- I never could find out what company that was. So then I wrote to Germany and I wrote to Buckeburg, which incidentally is now named Rhineburg. They changed the name. But anyway, they had a woman bürgermeister, and she went and she Xeroxed it apparently out of a book and she sent it to me. It was a flag of -- she said the company is still in business and everything. They dredge rivers and stuff like that. And they were using that houseboat as an office probably. Anyway, I said, okay, I got the guys' names, see. So I send it to the CEO and I said, "Hey, I got two flags of yours." I said -- I says, "Send me a ticket to Frankfurt and I will be glad to bring them back." And he -- I got the letter back saying something to the effect that, no, we don't need them that badly. Anyway, then after that, things got a little more difficult. But -- everybody went across Germany going east towards Berlin. We did a right move and started going south into the rural pocket. And then when we were in this town of Ketzerbachtal, that was the -- that was one of the worst days of my life, outside of Ketzerbachtal. We were going up the road and we found out -- I looked over, and I says, "There's C Company. I says, "We're leading the attack in a two-and-a-half-ton truck pulling antitank on you." And pretty soon bullets go through the canvas. And we go up this rise and one of our tanks is there, get hit -- and it catches on fire. It took -- all of the guys got out. Nobody got hurt and they all got out. And it stayed there and burned all day. So we set up our gun next to a little flimsy old gas station there. And the road divided like -- that was like the end of a Y. And it went downhill, see. But you couldn't see the bottom of the hill from where we were. And anyway, so I am standing there, and all of sudden, cement flies by my head. And there's two Germans, and one must have splutters and shot, but he missed. He hit the ground and stayed there. And they ran in -- they ran into these houses, see. They ran into these houses. So Creech and Rennie say, "We'll get them. We'll get them around the back." So they go around and they go down this little alleyway and they poke their heads over and, sure enough, there's the two Germans. They are standing in the field with some civilians. But the civilians spotted them right away and get out of there. He threw a grenade in there and they came back all shook up. And I said, "Well, why didn't you let them alone." Anyway, so later on that day, there's a German 88 apparently at the foot of that hill and he is firing direct fire at us, you know. The German 88 was firing at us directly and it really chopped up the building behind us and the one next to that. And later on at one of our association reunions in Spokane, my platoon leader was from there, Lieutenant McKelvy. And I said, "Where the hell were you when all that was going on?" And he said he was in that house. He said it apparently belonged to a dentist. He said there was all kind of dental equipment around and the guy was laying there. He shot himself, the German. He said he was in that house and he wanted -- he says he started hearing these voices, and it scared the hell out of him. It turns out that that is those tankers, that they came out of that tanker in the basement there. But, anyway, here comes this guy. He has got an Army uniform on with captain's bars, okay. So -- but he was a Navy guy. So this guy comes up and he says, "We will catch those two guys." So he says -- he grabs Street and Vaughn and he starts -- they don't get twenty feet and those shells come up there, whoop, hit that house. I hear screeches -- screaming over there. And we go over and pull them out from all this bricks and plaster and everything to come down. But anyway, this guy got a piece of shrapnel and he got a cut in the back of the neck. And he says, "Well, boys, that is enough for me." And we never saw that guy again. As fast as he came, he was gone again. I think it was a Navy guy that was just wearing an Army uniform that was with these -- I told you when they were working on the Rhine crossing. But he disappeared and we never saw him again. Then the rest of that -- oh, I know what happened. I am laying there. I am laying there and here comes three civilians, two men and a woman. And, of course, I imagine this -- I almost had my ears parted, you know. I am laying there and I had a -- I carry a .45 in a shoulder holster. So they are coming up there screaming at me in German, and I am not having it and I don't know what the hell they are talking about. So I pull out my .45 and they understood that right away and took off, see. Whatever they were doing out there, these people, bullets flying around and everything else, I don't know what they were doing. But anyway, later on that day, so we moved out. And when we were moving out, I just saw those two German guys. Someone nailed them. It must have been C Company -- C company was on our left flank and they came up and they must have nailed them because I saw the two guys lying there. Someone had did a number on them. But that was about -- that was about the last action. Then after that, we moved and then the glorious day came. It was May the 8th. The war is over. Baby, that is great. So we were actually out of commission -- we were actually sort of in reserve or out of small arms fire or harm's way at the time when that happened. So it was an anticlimax but welcome, nevertheless. That is all we were looking for. In the infantry, you only have two things to look forward to, the end of the war or a nice clean wound that puts you in the hospital until the end of the war. Nowadays they rotate people and that sort of thing. They did that in World War II for the Air Corps. The guys in the bomber and all of that, after so many missions, they go home for a furlough before they go back again. But in infantry, I had absolutely nothing to look forward to except a nice -- And the unfortunate part about it, you know, they say you find that bullet that has got your number on it and if you stay long enough -- I had a friend that -- a neighborhood kid that went from Africa, all the way from Africa up through Italy and everything and finally bought the farm in Germany probably a couple of weeks before the war was over. He had been there that long. Like I said, you had nothing to look forward to, but anyway --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies in your outfit, any close buddies?

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: No. Except my -- oh, I had wounded ones. That's all. They all got shrapnel, the sergeant, Mike, at least a half a dozen. I get hit, but it was spent. Street and I were sitting -- it is the first time I ever heard a German Nebelwerfer. That is a combination of tubes. And some people call them Screaming Mimi's because of the noise that they made. That was outside in Colmar. We were sitting on the edge of a gravel pit just in the morning. We hear this sound I had never heard before. Next thing you know, something had bounced -- fortunately, it had reached the end, both of us. Just bounced off of my overcoat and fell on the ground. I could see it there. It was a red hot piece. I couldn't get it for a souvenir. It was red hot. Any, I was going to tell you -- oh, I know what, what happened in the course of the events on our way to the Castrop-Rauxel. We overrun -- we overrun -- we overran a factory. It was an aluminum factory, perfect order. Steam still in the pipes, phones still working. Well, that was until we get done yelling obscenities over the phone. The German -- operators caught on and then they -- and then they wouldn't answer the phone. But anyway, I often wondered -- I often wondered what American corporation owned it. It was -- from a distance, from a couple of blocks away, it looked like a huge pile of coal. They had netting strung all over with little black paper hanging down, you know. Like I said, from a couple of blocks away, it looked like a huge pile of coal. It had never been touched by a bomb. This thing was in perfect working order. It was making aluminum, I guess. But anyway, that happened before we went to -- Castrop-Rauxel is -- we overran that and went in this German woodvin (phonetically) quarters, you know. It was something like we went in this office and like in Hollywood with tufted doors and all of that kind of stuff, you know. And Creech and I went in it. So we start splitting the closets. And he comes up with -- he comes up with a rifle and a pouch and I come up with two bottles of champagne. And then we found a safe, and we beat it open, but there was nothing in it but papers. But the funny thing about it was I read in the Stars and Stripes a little later about GIs scattering that kind of stuff all over to make it difficult for G2 to find all the evidence and papers and that sort of thing. But it also had a wine cellar with gigunda casks of wine down there, hundreds of bottles of wine. So we were down there, just break the neck and take a sip. Before we got out of there, there was all glass and wine all over the floor. But later on that day, that is a very bad day after that. But after that, the war was over. So they moved us to a town called -- oh, gee, I probably should get my book out. I can't think of the town. Can I --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: Let me get that book out. Dahlburg (phonetically).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Dahlburg (phonetically). Was that in Germany?

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: Yeah. This is south -- this was south of the Ruhr River, now. It's a small town south of the Ruhr River, okay? So then we were going to set up like occupation duty, you know. Of course, they said no fraternization. You're not supposed to talk to the people or anything. So what the guys did was they kind of roamed the streets and looked for German deserters and so forth and then searched the houses for weapons and that sort of duty. But I got the duty, because of Lieutenant McKelvy kind of forced it on me, there was a camp attached to this factory that was there that was full of Russians and Poles, slave labor. And then there was another sort of empty barracks and so forth. So what they decided to do was to pick up the -- the war is over now and these people were leaving Germany. They just picked up whatever bags they had and took off. So they were crowding all the roads and everything else. So they figured, well, the people -- the western Europeans, like the Dutch and the French and Belgium, they would pick them up. When we would get enough -- when we would get enough there for a boxcar load or something, they would take them to a railhead and ship them off and get them out of the way. Now, the Russians and the Poles were going nowhere. But then I was like -- called messermeister. I had to go get them food. So -- and the food had to be provided by the Germans. So we get German Army stores, you know, and get down and get dehydrated onions and dehydrated vegetables. And then the bread, I think it was like -- it was three-quarters sawdust. There was that bread. And I would go down and get these gigunda sacks of flour and have these guys take them to the next town to a bakery and then go back a day or two later and pick up about three hundred loaves of this bread. You could see the truck. They'd go down when you loaded it on there. But anyway, I would take it back. And I had help. I picked up -- I picked up an Italian PW, POW, and he spoke German very well. That is how he got caught in Germany when it capitulated, and they put him in a camp. And he said one day while he was working there, one of the guards hit him in the back with a boulder. And he said after that he kind of stuttered, you know. So anyway, I would -- I spoke Italian at the time. So I would talk to him or I would -- when I got down there dickering with these German people, he would listen in and then, you know, nudge me or tell me in Italian what was going on. So then I would do the proper screaming if I thought we were getting screwed or something like that. Wait a minute. And they would get the message. Anyway, that is the duty I pulled there. I had another camp in the town of Siegen, so I had actually three of those. But they -- you know, like, for instance, the Russians and the Poles already had -- you already had a guy like a Kapo who was a kind of leader. I would bring this stuff in and say, "Hey, look, you make sure these people all take a bath, you do this, you do that." I said, "Now here is your stores for a week." I say, "You divvy this up so that it lasts that long because that is it." So that is about all I did, and I stayed down at the camp. I had a room there and they would bring me my food and everything from our mess. They would bring it down there in mermite cans. But anyway, that was something else. I had -- oh, I got candy. And I would give it to the little two-year-old Russian girls. And so I would give them the candy. And now, another thing that happened, they bring in this French lady. She is about ready to drop her kid, you know. And I didn't want to be in -- so I go and I get a German doctor and bribe him with a pack of cigarettes, you know, "Come down and take a look at this lady." Fortunately they got her out of there before she delivered. So I got rid of that headache. But we did that and it didn't seem very long and then they pulled us all out. They pulled us all out of Germany, and we went back near Reims, France. And they took the division and divided up into -- I think it was about twenty-one camps and they were all named after towns. Camp Boston was kind of the headquarters. We were at Camp Boston. There was Pittsburgh, Cleveland, so forth, New Orleans. And we go back there and we pulled duty there. We were redeployed. Guys coming out of Germany. You would -- the guys with a lot of points that were going home for discharge, guys that were going to go to the Pacific directly through the Suez Canal, guys that were going to go home first to have a furlough before they went to the Far East because the war in Japan was still going on. So this was kind of a pretty good duty. If you didn't have some duty, though, what you would do is you chase PWs. You have to go down to the compound, pick up some prisoners. And, you know, if you had ditches to dig or something, they would do that kind of physical labor. But I worked for the lieutenant, so old McKelvy was in charge of the officers' club and mess, combination officers' club and mess. And he says, "Hey, I want you to decorate the place." Okay. I said, "okay, whatever." So I go down there and I start painting. I think it was Sad Sack chasing a woman with not too much clothing on, see. And that colonel came and he didn't appreciate the artwork. So I was down there the next day with a blowtorch taking it off. He said, "We'll get something a little more prosaic, if you want to call it. Paint in between all the windows -- paint the insignia of everybody that eats here." So you had crossed rifles and that sort of thing. Okay. I wound up doing that. Anyway, then he added two more things. He says, "Now I want you to take all the officers' dry cleaning into Reims and then pick it up." He says, "Go to a motor pool and get a driver and a Jeep. You take it in and then a couple of days later you go back and get it." Then he adds another one. He says, "Now, these guys would like to have fresh vegetables." So he says, "Now I want you to go to French farmers and buy tomatoes and stuff." So that was another part of my duties. So I go down and get a Jeep and a driver and a guy would chauffeur me around. So I got to go to Reims and stop at the Red Cross. That is where they signed the declaration, in that schoolhouse in Reims. You could see the Reims Cathedral, which is still beat up from World War I, still had scaffolding there that they were repairing from damage in World War I. And around that whole area you could still see remnants of trenches and stuff from the first war world. It was kind of interesting. But then I went to Madam Cheri. They had a farm and I would go down to the farm and buy the vegetables for the table. And I would go get the -- go get the dry cleaning. Got myself a nice jacket, a nice tanker jacket. Someone never picked it up, so I just appropriated it from the dry cleaning bit. I went on furlough then. That is another thing that happened. We drew lots, who was going to get the first furlough, see, and I won. But unfortunately, the first sergeant turned it in backwards. That means me last. So I went down there and I screamed. I said, "Hey, what do you mean? I won this thing. I'm supposed to be first." He says, "Oh, I already cut the papers. You will get the next one." Well, the first furlough was to the French Riviera. You get to fly down there and fly back. But then the next one that came up was for London. And I said, "Well, in the Army you don't pass up, you know, bird in hand." I says, "Give me that one." So I went to London for a week. And then I didn't -- I didn't bother coming back -- oh, that is another thing. When you were there and you got paid in French francs, you were actually getting screwed by your government if you spent your money there. It was hardly worth the fifty bucks of what we were getting, fifty-five dollars. I forget how much we were getting. It was hardly worth that on anything that you bought because of the inflated -- so the French started throwing in, I forget, maybe a thousand francs or something extra in everybody's pay to make up for that. But the smart thing to do was to take your entire pay, send it home in a money order. Then you got the full value of it, see, and then you lived off the black market. Because you could sell a pack -- a carton of cigarettes was a thousand francs to a Frenchman. But a thousand francs, if you took it and sent it home, was twenty dollars. You could change it to twenty dollars. So I got involved in a little bit of black market that way. That kept me in pocket money. And I sent my whole checks home to my mother. And I went to London, and I come back -- I went to the PX there and I came back with -- actually, I got back in camp because I stopped in Paris. We had -- we had trucks that left at 6:00 in the morning, would take you to Paris and then pick you up at midnight and come back. So if you weren't doing anything or if you could get a leave, you could take off and go to Paris. But Paris was extremely expensive, see. So what I would manage to do the times that we went there was to find a place, a GI place -- and they never questioned you -- and go in their mess lines and eat for nothing. Because if you ate in a restaurant, it would cost you a fortune. Anyway, I did that in London. When I come back, I got off the train and I said, "Oh, I think I will take the midnight one." Because you went across the Channel and you got on a truck to Paris. "So, I think I will spend a day in Paris and get on the midnight truck and go back." So they had -- the motor pool was in the -- it was called Les Invalides. Napoleon's tomb was there. And they had this gigunda area and there was all trucks parked in every place like a gigunda parking lot with trucks going all over the place. So I got off. And sure enough, if you are standing there and you have got your musette bag hanging on your shoulder, generally somebody gets the message. A guy says, "Yeah, yeah, I got some cigarettes to sell." So he said -- that was a kid. He said, "Okay, come with me." So I'm on the Left Bank -- and honest to god, I go through this entryway and I get in there and it is something like you see in Hollywood, big circular marble, a big circular staircase and everything else. I have never seen anything like it. A guy comes down. We made the deal. I got my money. I gave him the cigarettes. Then I went back to camp and I had more money than what I started out with. But I got to Paris. As a matter of fact, I was in Paris on V-J Day. And there wasn't too much celebration or anything. I went once -- a gang of us went once and we went to the Follies and that was an eye-opener, you know. You go to the Follies and it is -- it is an extravaganza like Radio City Music Hall. The only thing is that the women don't wear anything from the waist up. But the amazing thing is hey, there's parents there with their kids and everybody else. So that that -- Oh, I forgot to tell you, that weekend we went in London, we went to see Phyllis Dixie. Now, Phyllis Dixie was the Gypsy Rose Lee of England and Great Britain. So that was -- she would take off all her clothes and stand up there in poses, Venice in chains, Venice free, and all this. But the best part of of it was the audience was ninety-nine percent GIs. The comments they made were funny. That was the best part of the show anyway. So I got to see Phyllis Dixie. I always use that as a good quiz question. Who is Phyllis Dixie? And I went to Paris, and I got another trip to Paris on an errand. That was good because I went with another guy in a Jeep. And we kind of toured all over Paris. And I saw parts of Paris that I hadn't seen before. And then one day, one day under the Eiffel Tower, they had -- every airplane that had been used in the war was there, that big exhibit of all of that. So I got to see all the planes and everything. We horsed around in Paris. But like I said, it was extremely -- it was very expensive for a GI. I would find those GI mess halls. Then I also, while I was in camp -- then when the lieutenant went on furlough, I didn't even bother to go to work. I just laid in the sack and listened to the radio every day until he got back. But oh, we got -- then the guys with -- they had the points were dropping by tens, I think. And they would cut off, you know, if -- I said, "Everybody with eighty points can't go anywhere now because you'll be leaving." Then the next time it would be, "Everybody with seventy points can't go." So you could get furloughs real easy now, you know. So I got a trip to Switzerland. So me and my buddy, Mike from New York, we went to Switzerland. But in Switzerland they would only let you take, exchange thirty-seven bucks. That is all they allowed you to spend there. So load up on cigarettes and everything else too. But we toured Switzerland. We had a good time. We was rowboating on Lake Geneva and all of that kind of stuff. And I spent most of my ration -- they gave us ration -- rations. I spent most of it on pastries and spent most of my money on that, except I got my mother a watch and I got another watch. So then went from there and then we were in these like hospital tents. They had wood halfway up the sides. And then you had all your cots spread out in there. And that was our quarters. But what we did was we went to Moyeuvre-Grande. They had a hospital there. They had thrown out double-decker beds, so we brought back the double-decker beds and, you know, just sleep in your sleeping bag on the springs. But we had -- but two guys could fit in a space where you had two cots now, so we opened up a big space in there. And they had these space heaters that burned gasoline in the back, so we had a like a little club. And we had a guy that was in special service and he came with some upholstered furniture, so we had a couple of easy chairs. And then we had to cook. And so whatever was on the menu for the next day, we would have that night. And it all started when somebody raided the kitchen and snuck in the kitchen, come back with a loin of pork chops. What the hell are you doing with pork chops? So they cut them up and fried them in their mess kits on top of that little stove. Then after that, the cook got into it. So he would provide us with whatever was going to be on the menu the next day. So we had like a little clubhouse. We would sit there and listen to the radio and play cards and while away the time. And other guys had -- some of the guys brought back prostitutes and had them -- they were pimping for them. We never had one in our tent, but they had them in other tents over there. And when the MPs decided to make a raid and you looked out in the field and you see all these women running across the field -- Then anyway, not much of else was going on except working over at the officers' club and going after the vegetables and so forth until the vegetable season was over. And then I got another -- around Christmastime I got another furlough to Switzerland, so I went back to Switzerland with another guy this time and I went to some different places. I went to Montreux. Montreux has the Castle of Chillon. And that is where Lord Byron carved his name in one of the posts in the dungeon on or whatever it was. So I scratched mine in below it, the Castle of Chillon. We had a good time there anyway. I come back, and by that time, it was the end of January after Christmas. I just hung around because now my number was coming up. So I could have gone back -- I could have gone back to Chamonix skiing, but I wasn't interested in skiing or anything. So anyway, I just waited my time until my points came up and then I transferred to -- I think it was called Camp Home Run in Le Havre. That is the first stepping stones to getting you home, you know. So we went and we spent -- we spent time there and it was -- well, it was really cold now. And they would only give you a bucket of coal. These stoves, you burn coal in them. So they only give you a bucket of coal. So what we would do is hang out in the Red Cross all day, drink coffee and eat donuts. And then at night, we would quickly burn up our ration and then go to sleep while it was still warm. And guys went out and chopped up trees and were burning trees. And I understand the U.S. Government had to pay the French afterwards for those trees that they chopped up. And then I went to -- I can't think of the name of it -- Saint Tot (inaudible) it is above Le Havre and it is like a moated fort. And they sent me there. And I had the duty of -- there was only one way in and one way out in this thing. And I had a duty there as mail clerk. And so I would go down -- you get a Jeep and a driver and go down in Le Havre. You get the mail, bring it back and distribute it. But most of the mail -- most of the mail just had to be readdressed because all these guys had all gone home, see. So I had two Germans. I had Willie and Max. One -- one told me he was a prisoner of World War I, he worked in a British mess. But Willie and Max knew more about what was going on than I did, so all I did was I would take them the stuff and they would readdress it all. I've still got a letter -- no, I -- I gave it to the Carlisle Barracks. It still had -- I got one of my own that was readdressed. And I had "Willie and Max, regards, we are still here." And I got that letter. So I had -- I had a soft touch there, sit around and I used to get these paperback books, but the war editions. I don't know if you have ever seen them. They are horizontal and they have two pages to -- on one page, in other words. And so they would send you a batch of them. I picked out the ones that I wanted to read. You know where they were going to. They were going to the officers' quarters. I'd pick out the ones I wanted to read and then let the guys get some they wanted to read. Then I would give them the rest of them because I knew that is what they were going to get. And they had the overseas edition of Time Magazine. So that's all you did, just lay around all day. That mail thing is -- and it was up in the PX up on a little mezzanine. And there was a couple of French girls there. They did manicures. So I would just there and BS with them all day. And the other guys were working. They had like a cage, like a regular postal cage, you know. And Willie and Max were doing the work, and I was just biding my time until it was time to go home. And then, see, I reversed that. Then I went to Camp Home Run and from there I went home. And before that, I missed a story about going to Luxembourg, Rennie and I, see. So Rennie gets a truck, ton-and-a-half ton truck and we are going to haul these guys to an airfield outside of Metz because they have so many points they are being flown home for discharge. And so -- so we take these guys and we drop them off. He says, "Hey, you know, we are not very far from Luxembourg." So I said, "Okay." So we take off and we go to Luxembourg City. And so it is kind of a nice way to see the scenery. And we stop at the Red Cross and had the usual coffee and donuts. And then I look and here is Rennie and he has got -- he has got this big red line running down his arm and he has got this lump under his arm. And I said, "What the hell is the matter with you?" You know, I said, "We are not supposed to be here, but you know what, I think we had better go check in at the dispensary, you know, and see a doctor." So we went in, even though we weren't supposed to be there. And the guy looked at it and he says, "Oh, you have got blood poison." And he says, "How far is it back to where you are going?" And we tell them, "Oh, we can get back by dark, you know." He said, "Okay, I will let you go then." And they did nothing. He says, "But when you get back there, you go to the hospital." "Okay, you go to the hospital and I will take the truck back to the motor pool," which is what we did. But then it went away and he didn't have much of a problem after that anyhow. Oh, now I am getting ready to leave. Okay. From Le Havre. So first I get a boat -- no. Here is what happens. I got more money. The government had instituted a currency control. See, they are supposed to know all the money you had. And, of course, when I sent mine -- when I sent mine home to my mother, they would erase that amount. So I didn't have much of anything on mine, but I had a lot of money in my pocket, see. So then I meet up with this guy from New York, a Mafia type. And I said, I said, "I tell you what," I said, "I will give you this money. Since you spent all your money," I said, "I will give you this money, you change it and then you gamble when we get on the ship." And I says, "If we win, we win; if we don't, we don't." I said, "The money is only going to be souvenir paper to me, these French francs when they exchange to American money." So he did that. He gets sick -- he gets sick before the boat even gets away from the pier. So I am carrying food down to him and everything. He didn't leave. He didn't leave. And now we were on -- we were on a ship, German ship captured in World War II off the coast of South America. And it is renamed the S.S. Lejeune and it is run by -- it is run by U.S. sailors and everything. And we are getting American food and it was lousy, I tell you. But anyway, so I endured that trip on the Lejeune. So we get back to the U.S. and we are at Camp Dix. And this guy tells me, he says, "Hey, my wife and kids are going to come down and she is going to drive them down to the camp and go home." And he says, "I don't need this money." So he gave me the money, so I'm about two hundred bucks to the good. I get discharged and the guy says, "Well, let's see, you were a gunner on a fifty-seven millimeter antitank gun. That doesn't transfer to any civilian jobs very good." So he says, "I will put you down for sign painter." And he put -- and so then I -- that is when I left and took a train home to Pennsylvania. That was the end of my Army career. I think I threw my overcoat away on the way home, but I kept the rest of the stuff. I kept my Ike jacket because I sold my Ike jacket later for fifteen bucks.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very good. Is there any other particularly vivid memory that comes to mind about your time overseas? That certainly sounds like you've covered it.

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: I think I covered most of it, yeah. I was just trying to think. No, I -- you know, these -- a couple of years ago, when I told you I found that postcard in that house, I finally made contact with the people that lived there. Yeah. The postcard on the back of it was French. And it had been from Uncle Teal to his niece and congratulating her on doing very well at nunnery school or whatever. So then I got a guy. He was kind of in charge of World War II museums or something in Belgium, see. And he went down there and he says, "Oh, yeah, these people are still living there" and gave me their address. So then I wrote to them and I took that postcard and I mounted it -- I mounted it in a frame with glass on both sides so you could see the front and the back, you know, and I sent it. The girl was now -- she was eighty-four years old and she was a nun. She's still teaching school. And when I got all this information and everything, I called the guy that writes for the Plain Dealer that handles war stories --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that Clint O'Connor?

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Bryan Albright, maybe?

sp.speaker: Lawrence Verga
sp.p: No, another name. But anyway, he told me, he says, "I am on the east side." The girl from Bay Village came out here and I told her the story. So she said, "Oh." I didn't know what she was going to do with it. And I showed her the thing and everything else. And so then one day she calls me and says, "Meet me up at Elyria there at the Plain Dealer offices that they have up there." So I go up there and she has made arrangements for a three-person call to Belgium. Yeah. So I had this nun on the other end, see. Well, they didn't know that I could understood French. But her mother taught French at the Gilmore Academy. So her mother was at Gilmore Academy on the phone and the two of us were on phones up here and the nun was on the phone in Belgium, so we had quite a chitchat. It was really interesting. She was really funny. I really liked her. I am sorry I didn't get over to see her. She passed away a couple of days before 9/11. But I am still in contact with -- the sister still lives in that house.
